title: The one the earth doesn't know
hookLine: Yajnavalkya names the one who lives in the earth, unknown to it
carry: the lord lives within you as inner controller
tomorrow: what if the line really says 'you are NOT that'?

lines: IN THE EARTH, UNKNOWN TO IT?
cards: A phone runs on code nobody using it ever sees. It's in every tap, and the phone has no idea. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad has a stranger sentence than that.

The father from the Chandogya, Uddalaka Aruni, presses the sage Yajnavalkya about the inner controller. The answer: the one who dwells in the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is.
How can something live in the earth, and the earth not know it?

teach.h: IN THE EARTH, UNKNOWN TO THE EARTH.
teach.b: In paraphrase, Yajnavalkya says: the one who dwells in the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who rules the earth from within, that is your self, the inner controller, the immortal.
Then he goes through water, fire, sky, wind, sun, breath, eye and mind, the same pattern each time. Here's the answer to the puzzle. A body doesn't have to know who lives in it to be lived in.
This is a big teaching for Sri Vaishnavas, the tradition of Ramanuja: the Lord, whom they worship as Narayana, lives within every being as the antaryami, the inner controller.

Ramanuja, the teacher of the Vishishtadvaita school, reads tat tvam asi through this passage. Everything, your own self included, is the body of Brahman, and Brahman lives in it as its inner self. Now think about names.
Say Devadatta, and you don't mean a body alone; you mean the person who has that body. So in Ramanuja's reading, you finally names Brahman too: Brahman as the one whose body you are.
That names Brahman as the cause of the world.

One reality, named two ways, and nothing set aside. Your self stays real, and stays yours, held as close as a body and the one who lives in it. For Ramanuja, the saying doesn't erase the one who hears it.
It tells them who lives within them.

how: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition that follows Ramanuja, the inner-controller passage of the Brihadaranyaka is studied as a key to reading the Upanishads, and the self is understood as the body of Brahman.

o: that you are: Brahman, dwelling in you as your self
that god lives far away, outside of you
you are the earth, and you are nothing more

games.q: the inner controller. tap the pairs.
p: doesn't know the one within it

s: every Hindu school reads tat tvam asi the same way
Advaita sets the labels aside; Ramanuja hears both words naming Brahman, with the self as its body.
in the Brihadaranyaka, the earth is called the inner controller's body
whose body the earth is, who rules it from within.

games.q: a friend says: if the divine really lived inside me, i'd feel it all the time. what does Yajnavalkya's answer suggest?
o: the earth doesn't know the one dwelling in it; a body needn't feel it.
you'd feel it every moment, or else it isn't there at all.
the inner controller lives only in sages, not in ordinary people.
games.why: the one who dwells in the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is. Ramanuja reads every self the same way.

practice: Sit tall and feel the body from the inside: the weight in the seat, the breath moving, the warmth in the hands. Let the ground under you and the air around you belong to the same picture.
If you pray, you can rest with the text's own words: the inner controller, the immortal.

wordCard.voice: Tat tvam asi, read Ramanuja's way: both words name Brahman, and you are the body the Lord dwells in.

orig.note: Sanskrit: antaryami, the inner controller in the Brihadaranyaka.

carryVoice: Here's the line: the Lord lives within you as the inner controller, even when you don't feel it. Talk soon.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.7.1–3 and following (Uddalaka Aruni asks Yajnavalkya about the inner controller; the one who dwells in the earth, other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who rules it from within: that is your self, the inner controller, the immortal)
Ramanuja, Vedartha Sangraha and Sri Bhashya on tat tvam asi (both words denote Brahman; 'tvam' denotes Brahman with the individual self as its body) — general
